Elicitation or Expansion? Demystifying Gains from Agent Harness Optimization

Younghyun Kim  , Wooseok Seo, Minseo Kim, Seunghyuk Oh, Minjae Lee
Donghoon Kim, Hyung Il Koo, Jaehyung Kim, Wonjun Kang
FuriosaAI Yonsei University University of California, Berkeley  Project page: furiosa-air.github.io/elicitation-or-expansion  Code: github.com/furiosa-ai/elicitation-or-expansion  Dataset: datasets/furiosa-ai/elicitation-or-expansion-trajectories ††thanks: Equal contribution.  ^†^{\dagger}Co-corresponding authors.
Abstract

Recent studies in harness optimization have shown substantial performance gains in language model agents without updating model weights. A well-designed harness more effectively leverages the underlying model’s capabilities by shaping context, tool use, and execution workflows. However, naïve success rates alone do not fully characterize whether optimized harness yields more reliable success on tasks already within reach (elicitation) or a broader range of solvable tasks (expansion). This distinction is crucial for recursive self-improvement and evolutionary search, as expansion may provide a broader range of successful experiences to push the capability boundaries. Despite the growing significance, this distinction remains underexplored in harness optimization. We conduct a systematic analysis to study the effect of gains from harness optimization. Building on pass​@​k\mathrm{pass@}k analyses in the reinforcement learning (RL) literature that compare models before and after RL training, we compare optimized harnesses with their pre-optimization counterparts. Specifically, we assess changes in reachable task coverage, compare harness optimization with model scaling and increased inference-time compute, and examine how gains vary with task difficulty. Across static prediction and dynamic tasks, we find that pass​@​1\mathrm{pass@}1 advantages of harness over stronger interventions can reverse at larger attempt budgets and aggregate gains conceal shortfalls on hard tasks, underscoring the need for a fine-grained diagnosis.

1 Introduction

The ability of a language model agent is influenced by the design of its harness, which governs prompting, context management, tool use, and execution logic (Young, 2025; OpenAI, 2026). Refining these components can substantially improve agent performance without updating model parameters, motivating growing interest in harness optimization. By broadening the scope of harness optimization beyond prompts (Agrawal et al., 2026) and context (Zhang et al., 2026d) to agent code and execution workflows (Hu et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2026b), recent methods have achieved huge performance gains across diverse tasks. However, these aggregate benchmark gains alone do not reveal which aspects of the agent system have improved. For instance, comparable gains arise either from simply reformatting otherwise correct answers to satisfy the evaluation protocol or from enabling the agent to more effectively leverage its environment and external feedback to deal with previously unsolved tasks. This distinction is especially important for approaches that leverage successful experience for subsequent improvement, including recursive self-improvement  (Zhang et al., 2026b; Lee et al., 2026a). In these settings, even rare successes on previously unreachable tasks can provide a foundation for further search or learning.

Recent studies have begun to examine the nature of harness gains by relating prompt edits to task-dependent performance changes (Gong & Wen, 2026), attributing improvements to recoverable execution defects (Yang et al., 2026), and comparing harness evolution with simple retries (Wang et al., 2026). However, these analyses leave open how task coverage under the original and optimized harnesses differs as the attempt budget increases. Whether the task coverage of optimized harness persists, disappears, or reverses matters for assessing how far the optimized harness can extend an agent’s practical problem-solving reach without further model training. A closely related debate in reinforcement learning (RL) provides a useful diagnostic perspective. Comparisons between RL-trained models and their pre-RL counterparts show that improvements in pass​@​1\mathrm{pass@}1 can diminish or reverse at larger sampling budgets, suggesting improved sampling efficiency rather than broader task coverage (Yue et al., 2025). Other studies report broader coverage under the valid reasoning evaluation (Wen et al., 2026) or additional tool use (Zhai et al., 2026), while controlled experiments show that coverage gains depend on pre-training exposure and training-task difficulty (Zhang et al., 2026a). Together, these studies lay the ground for examining how improvements behave across sampling budgets and task conditions, rather than inferring their nature from a single aggregate score.

In this work, we investigate whether harness optimization makes success more frequent on tasks already solved by the baseline (elicitation) or broadens observed task coverage (expansion) through the lens of pass​@​k\mathrm{pass@}k (Chen et al., 2021). We complement this analysis by comparing optimized harnesses with base harness using larger models from the same family or higher reasoning effort. These baselines provide empirical reference for assessing how far harness optimization alone enhances an agent’s capability. Finally, we examine whether gains are concentrated on easier tasks or extend to harder ones. Figure 1 depicts why these multi-axis analyses matter. Here, overall pass​@​1\mathrm{pass@}1 gain does not fully characterize harness gains; the optimized harness leaves the agent less capable of solving harder problems than under the original harness. Our analysis thus unveils concealed coverage loss on harder tasks.11 1 This example uses an optimized harness under relaxed per-attempt resource limits in Appendix C.4

The heterogeneous effects recur throughout our analyses on various benchmarks. First, advantages over stronger references can reverse as the attempt budget increases: on LawBench (Fei et al., 2024), the optimized GPT-OSS-20B harness exceeds the GPT-OSS-120B baseline by 16.0516.05 percentage points (pp) at pass​@​1\mathrm{pass@}1, but trails it by 4.004.00 pp at pass​@​64\mathrm{pass@}64. Second, on HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018) and AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024), the selected harnesses approach or exceed stronger references in aggregate but do not surpass them on hard subsets. Third, the transferred text-classification harness falls below its baseline at pass​@​64\mathrm{pass@}64 on all out-of-distribution datasets, despite small pass​@​1\mathrm{pass@}1 gains on two. This heterogeneity makes systematic analysis necessary: understanding harness gains requires distinguishing reliability from coverage and examining how both change across attempt budgets, task groups, reference systems.

2 Related Work

2.1 Harness Optimization

Harness optimization adapts agent’s prompts, context, and execution logic through repeated evaluation and revision. TextGrad (Yuksekgonul et al., 2025) and GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2026) refine prompts through natural-language feedback, while ACE (Zhang et al., 2026d) incorporates lessons from execution into an evolving context playbook. Methods that search over agent code (Hu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026e) use execution feedback to diagnose failures and guide revisions across harness components (Lin et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026c; Park et al., 2026; Yue et al., 2026). Our study focuses on Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026b), which uses a coding-agent proposer to selectively inspects prior harness code, evaluation scores, and execution traces for new candidates.

2.2 Interpreting Capability Gains

Analyses of reinforcement learning show that higher pass​@​1\mathrm{pass@}1 can accompany reduced coverage at large sampling budgets (Yue et al., 2025), while other studies find broader coverage under different training and evaluation conditions (Wen et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a). Recent work further documents smaller gains on harder problems under standard reinforcement learning and shows that adaptive sampling can improve learning on these problems (Noukhovitch et al., 2026). Studies of repeated sampling (Brown et al., 2024) and agent interaction budgets (Zhai et al., 2026) examine how additional attempts and interactions affect coverage, while test-time scaling analyses show that effective compute allocation depends on task difficulty (Snell et al., 2025). For harness optimization, analyses compare evolution with test-time search (Wang et al., 2026), trace gains to execution repairs (Yang et al., 2026), and examine the repeatability (Zhao et al., 2026) and model dependence (Lin et al., 2026b) of improvements. We analyze optimized harnesses across attempt budgets and difficulty levels, distinguishing coverage gains over the original baseline from advantages that persist against baselines with larger models or more inference compute.

3 Analysis Setup

3.1 Preliminary: Harness Optimization

Let MM denote a solver model and HH its harness, which controls model inputs, tool interactions, and execution state. On a task xx, executing (ℳ,H)(\mathcal{M},H) yields a complete trajectory τ∼πℳ,H(⋅∣x)\tau\sim\pi_{\mathcal{M},H}(\cdot\mid x), evaluated by a task-specific scoring function r⁡(τ,x)r(\tau,x). Given a task distribution 𝒳\mathcal{X}, harness optimization seeks to maximize the expected task score J⁡(ℳ,H)J(\mathcal{M},H) by revising HH while keeping ℳ\mathcal{M} fixed:

maxHJ(ℳ,H),J(ℳ,H)=𝔼x∼𝒳,τ∼πℳ,H(⋅∣x)[r(τ,x)].\max_{H}\;J(\mathcal{M},H),\qquad J(\mathcal{M},H)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{X},\,\tau\sim\pi_{\mathcal{M},H}(\cdot\mid x)}\bigl[r(\tau,x)\bigr].

For our main experiments, we use Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026b), whose coding agent, called proposer, selectively inspects previous harness code, evaluation scores, and execution traces to diagnose failures and propose revised harnesses. Each candidate is evaluated, and its code and execution feedback are retained to guide subsequent proposals. Our analysis compares the initial harness H0H_{0} with an optimized harness H⋆H^{\star} selected based on validation performance. We estimate their pass​@​k\mathrm{pass@}k from repeated executions on a common test set under the same task-specific scorer (Appendix A).

3.2 Motivation: Beyond Mean Accuracy

For a fixed set of tasks and number of attempts (kk) per task, pass​@​1\mathrm{pass@}1 determines the expected number of successful executions (i.e., mean accuracy), whereas pass​@​k\mathrm{pass@}k measures the expected fraction of tasks solved at least once in kk complete executions (Chen et al., 2021) (i.e., coverage). A harness can therefore achieve higher mean accuracy but low coverage, by repeatedly solving the same tasks without obtaining successes on additional ones. When generated solutions are used for self-training (Zelikman et al., 2022) or verifier-based selection (Cobbe et al., 2021), coverage is particularly important as it captures the breadth of tasks for which a successful example or solution is available.

Figure 2 compares pass​@​1\mathrm{pass@}1 and pass​@​128\mathrm{pass@}128 for Qwen3-8B harness candidates from one optimization run, each evaluated on the same 300 HotpotQA tasks with k=128k=128 executions per task. Although the two metrics broadly track one another, the candidate with the highest estimated pass​@​1\mathrm{pass@}1 differs from the one with the highest observed pass​@​128\mathrm{pass@}128. Repeated evaluation can improve the precision of pass​@​1\mathrm{pass@}1, but does not make it a substitute for measuring task coverage at larger budgets.

4 Evaluation Setup

We refer to (ℳ,H0)(\mathcal{M},H_{0}) and (ℳ,H⋆)(\mathcal{M},H^{\star}) as the baseline and optimized system, respectively. The reference (ℳref,H0)(\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{ref}},H_{0}) uses the base harness with a larger solver model or the same solver model at higher reasoning effort. We compare each system on a large kk attempts. More details are in Appendix B.

4.1 Static Tasks

Text classification. Following Lee et al. (2026b), we jointly optimize a single harness across three static prediction datasets: Symptom2Disease (Gretel AI, 2023) for diagnosis from symptom descriptions, LawBench (Fei et al., 2024) for charge-set prediction, and USPTO (Schneider et al., 2016) for reactant-SMILES set prediction. In these tasks, the harness constructs reference context to support prediction. We use a few-shot harness as H0H_{0}, since directly supplying labeled examples provides a simple way to construct such context. The optimized harness H⋆H^{\star} prepares memory from the same pool and retrieves relevant information to construct context for each test input. Across repetitions, H0H_{0} resamples demonstrations and H⋆H^{\star} rebuilds memory (Appendix C.2). For out-of-distribution (OOD) transfer, we reuse H⋆H^{\star} obtained from in-distribution (ID) datasets to FiNER (Loukas et al., 2022), GoEmotions (Demszky et al., 2020), and Banking77 (Casanueva et al., 2020). We use GPT-OSS-20B (Agarwal et al., 2025) as ℳ\mathcal{M} and GPT-OSS-120B as ℳref\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{ref}} for comparison.

4.2 Dynamic Tasks

Multi-hop QA. On HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018), the harness coordinates evidence retrieval and answer generation. The base harness H0H_{0} follows multi-hop program of GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2026): it retrieves passages, generates a follow-up query from the retrieved evidence, and answers using summaries accumulated across the two retrieval rounds. We obtain H⋆H^{\star} by optimizing the harness code governing query construction, evidence processing, and answer generation, while keeping the BM25 retriever fixed. Evaluation uses 300 test questions with their original difficulty labels. We use Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025) as ℳ\mathcal{M} and Qwen3-32B as ℳref\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{ref}} for comparison.

Agentic task. On AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024), the harness coordinates multi-turn interactions with simulated applications, where actions change the environment and execution feedback informs subsequent decisions. The baseline harness H0H_{0} follows the benchmark’s simplified ReAct implementation (Yao et al., 2023), alternating Python code generation and execution. Evaluation uses the 168 tasks in test_normal with their original difficulty labels. We use GPT-OSS-120B for both ℳ\mathcal{M} and ℳref\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{ref}}. The solver’s reasoning effort is fixed at medium during harness optimization and for the base and optimized systems; the reference system uses high reasoning effort.

6 Conclusion

We provide a diagnostic lens for understanding what harness optimization improves, where its gains persist, and where performance shortfalls remain. By combining pass​@​k\mathrm{pass@}k curves with stronger reference systems and analyses across task difficulty, we distinguish more reliable success from broader observed task coverage. These diagnostics help assess whether a harness suits an intended attempt budget and task group.

Limitations and future work. Achieving consistent capability expansion on hard tasks remains an important open challenge for harness optimization, especially when successful executions support recursive self-improvement or evolutionary search. This motivates search and selection methods that reward validated successes on previously uncovered hard tasks and retain candidates with complementary successes. Large-budget pass​@​k\mathrm{pass@}k analysis provides a diagnostic basis. Our experimental results are bounded by the evaluated benchmarks, solver families, and optimization runs examined in this study.

Appendix A Repeated Evaluation and pass​@​k\mathrm{pass@}k

We repeat complete executions of each fixed solver–harness pair on the same NN test tasks, including all internal model calls and tool interactions. Let nn be the number of rollouts and cic_{i} be the number of successes of task xix_{i}. We estimate coverage within kk attempts following Chen et al. (2021):

pass​@​k^​(M,H)=1N​∑i=1N[1−(n−cik)(nk)],1≤k≤n,\hat{\mathrm{pass@}k}(M,H)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[1-\frac{\binom{n-c_{i}}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}}\right],\qquad 1\leq k\leq n, (1)

where the numerator is zero when n−ci<kn-c_{i}<k. Tasks are weighted equally within each dataset or benchmark; text macro averages weight datasets equally. At k=1k=1, this is mean task success; at k=nk=n for equal-sized pools, it is the fraction solved at least once. Equation 1 is unbiased under independent, identically distributed attempts from a fixed policy.

Appendix B Experimental Details

B.1 Datasets and Splits

We follow prior split protocols, with sample sizes and adaptations in Table 1. Symptom2Disease, LawBench, USPTO, and FiNER use the MCE splits (Ye et al., 2026) distributed with Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026b); GoEmotions (Demszky et al., 2020) and Banking77 (Casanueva et al., 2020) derive from their public releases. We subsample only examples with one annotated label from official splits for GoEmotions to ease the evaluation. HotpotQA follows GEPA’s split sizes (Agrawal et al., 2026) using disjoint subsets of the official fullwiki training set. AppWorld retains the official train, development, and test_normal partitions (Trivedi et al., 2024). Both dynamic benchmarks retain their original difficulty labels.

B.2 Baselines and Harness Optimization

We use Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026b) with Claude Opus 5 as the coding-agent proposer, keeping solver weights fixed. Each optimization allows 20 iterations with up to two proposals per iteration.

Text classification.

We use GPT-OSS-20B for the baseline and optimized harness, with GPT-OSS-120B as the stronger reference; all use medium reasoning effort and temperature 0. Both baselines adapt the few-shot harness of Lee et al. (2026b), resampling demonstrations for each query and repetition within a pre-defined character budget. We select by equal-dataset mean validation accuracy. The selected harness rebuilds memory from preparation examples for each repetition. OOD evaluation uses GPT-OSS-20B with the same preparation policy on target-domain examples, without further code optimization.

HotpotQA.

We use Qwen3-8B with Qwen3-32B as the stronger reference, both at temperature 0.6. The baseline follows GEPA’s multihop seed program (Agrawal et al., 2026) with BM25 retrieval. The optimized harnesses are capped at four solver calls, two retrievals, and seven passages per retrieval as well as the baseline. We shortlist candidates using validation performance and select by exact match (EM) on a separate selection set.

AppWorld.

We use GPT-OSS-120B at medium reasoning effort, with a high-effort baseline as the stronger reference. Repeated evaluation uses temperature 1. The baseline ports AppWorld’s simplified ReAct agent (Trivedi et al., 2024). Each attempt permits 50 solver calls and 50 environment steps, with a 2,400-second timeout extended to 7,200 seconds for high effort. Search and selection use temperature zero and original TGC, with final selection on the development set.

B.3 Success Scorers

We apply the same scorer to all systems within each benchmark, relaxing format requirements where necessary to better distinguish task completion from format compliance. In text classification, we use binary correctness after dataset-specific surface normalization. In HotpotQA, to accept correct answers embedded in longer responses, we use Judge=(Contain∧CORRECT)\mathrm{Judge}=(\mathrm{Contain}\land\mathrm{CORRECT}): answer containment with an LLM judgment confirming correctness. Table 2 gives examples that illustrate the failure mode from the Qwen3-32B baseline in Figure 6. Each complete response states the reference answer but receives EM = 0. With 128 attempts per task, EM gives the Qwen3-32B lower pass​@​1\mathrm{pass@}1 than Qwen3-8B, which is counterintuitive, whereas Judge reverses this ordering. In AppWorld, we use arity-fixed TGC: original successes remain successful, and an action attempt is additionally accepted only if all state checks pass, no execution error is recorded, and its sole failed check concerns an unrequested answer. With 128 attempts per task, original TGC ranks the GPT-OSS-120B below GPT-OSS-20B at pass​@​1\mathrm{pass@}1; arity-fixed TGC reverses this ordering.

Appendix C Additional Experimental Results

C.1 Variation Across Optimization Runs

We repeat harness optimization three times per benchmark and evaluate the selected harness from each run. Figure 12 shows the mean and sample standard deviation (SD) across runs. Evaluation uses 64 attempts per task for text classification and 128 for HotpotQA and AppWorld. Mean gains over the original baseline shrink from pass​@​1\mathrm{pass@}1 to the largest evaluated budget in all three benchmarks. The amount of the gain varies across runs, but improved single-attempt success does not consistently yield an advantage over stronger references at larger budgets. In text classification, all three optimized systems fall below the larger-model reference at pass​@​64\mathrm{pass@}64. On hard HotpotQA and AppWorld tasks, none exceeds the larger-model or higher-effort reference, respectively, anywhere along the evaluated curves. SD includes evaluation and preparation; it does not isolate optimizer variance.

C.2 Static Tasks

Additional results on GPT-OSS-120B.

Single-attempt gains also do not improve pass​@​64\mathrm{pass@}64 for GPT-OSS-120B. In Figure 13, LawBench pass​@​1\mathrm{pass@}1 increases from 27.95%27.95\% to 38.66%38.66\%, while pass​@​64\mathrm{pass@}64 decreases from 60%60\% to 59%59\%. The optimized harness also has lower pass​@​64\mathrm{pass@}64 on Symptom2Disease, and its USPTO curve remains below the baseline throughout.

Task-level changes in observed success sets.

Net coverage changes on the static tasks combine newly solved and lost tasks across each dataset, as shown in Table 3.

Frozen memory.

Reusing one prepared memory across repetitions, instead of rebuilding it for each repetition, leaves the pattern in Figure 4 (a)-(c) unchanged, as shown in Table 4. With either memory policy, the selected GPT-OSS-20B harness improves pass​@​1\mathrm{pass@}1 over H0H_{0} on all three datasets, while at pass​@​64\mathrm{pass@}64 it falls below H0H_{0} on Symptom2Disease, its LawBench gain narrows, and it remains below the GPT-OSS-120B reference on every dataset.

Random guessing on static tasks.

Both harnesses exceed uniform-guessing coverage on the four single-label datasets at smaller kk, as shown in Table 5. Independent uniform guesses over LL labels yield expected coverage 1−(1−1/L)k1-(1-1/L)^{k}.

C.3 Dynamic Tasks

We also optimize a harness for GPT-OSS-20B on each dynamic benchmark, as shown in Figure 14. The optimized system exceeds the 120B baseline on HotpotQA at pass​@​128\mathrm{pass@}128 (89.00%89.00\% versus 85.33%85.33\%), while remaining slightly below it on AppWorld at pass​@​64\mathrm{pass@}64 (91.07%91.07\% versus 91.67%91.67\%).

Optimization with aligned scorers.

We repeat optimization and selection with the success scorers defined in Appendix B.3. We retain the original test sets and difficulty groups and evaluate through k=128k=128. Figures 15 and 16 are consistent with the main findings in Section 5.2. Overall gains over the original baselines narrow from pass​@​1\mathrm{pass@}1 to pass​@​128\mathrm{pass@}128, while the displayed harnesses remain below the larger-model or higher-effort reference on hard tasks throughout kk.

C.4 Optimization Conditions

Relaxed resource limits do not yield higher mean coverage at k=128k=128 in these runs. We compare three Qwen3-8B optimization runs per setting, with caps of 4 solver calls, 2 retrievals, and 7 passages per retrieval (tight) versus 12/12/20 (relaxed). Each run proposes 40 candidates on the same optimization splits; the caps apply during both optimization and evaluation.
